newsitem.title: FINLAND: IHALAINEN SAYS SUPPORTS LIPPONEN, GOVT ECON POLICY.
newsitem.headline: IHALAINEN SAYS SUPPORTS LIPPONEN, GOVT ECON POLICY.

text.p: Lauri Ihalainen, chairman of the Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions (SAK), was on Monday quoted as saying that he strongly supports Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen and the government's economic policy.
"One must state emphatically that the main direction of the economic policy is corredct," Ihalainen said in an interview in social democratic daily Demari.

It would be more important to focus on measures aiming at achieving a permanent turn for the better in employment than to stare at the government's official target to halve unemployment by the end of its term in 1999, he said.
"Rapid growth, 3-5 percent, is a fundamental condition for an improvement in employment, but an insufficient condition to halve unemployment by the year 2000," Ihalainen said.
"We need long-term stability in our economic policy and the political nerves to implement it," he said.

With its 1.1 million mainly blue-collar members, SAK is Finland's biggest trade union group. Most of its leaders, including Ihalainen, belong to the social democratic party (SDP), of which prime minister Lipponen is chairman.
Ihalainen said SDP should remain in government because neo-liberalism was lurking around the corner.
Key issues like employment, Economic and Monetary Union, the next pay deal and how to maintain and reform the welfare state needed to be addressed.
"Without the social democrats, a balanced and fair treatment of these issues would be impossible," he said.
"Neo-liberalism is waiting around the corner hoping that the social democrats will fail," he added.
SDP should now unite to overcome internal strife.
"Now is the time to come together, admit mistakes, but also respect each other and decide that the responsibility of government will be shouldered until the end," Ihalainen said.
Viewed against expectations, many social democrats were disappointed with the SDP-led government and SAK, too, was not pleased with a number of decisions, he said.
But social democratic policy should not fluctuate with every cyclical swing and not become entangled in the first difficulties, Ihalainen added.
The problems simmering under the surface had come to light in parliament's rejection of a government proposal to allow retail stores to be open for business on Sundays, he said.
He said he was no friend of Sunday open and that he thought SAK-members were able to spend their earnings in six days.

Referring to Lipponen's decision to hand the proposal back to parliament and turn the issue into a vote of confidence, Ihalainen said he hoped it would be possible to agree on such adjustments that the proposal would work better in practice.
In the confidence vote, "The continuation of credible cooperation will be at stake," he said.
